::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Two drops touching do not merge instantly. A film of air has to drain out first, and what happens next can leave a smaller drop behind.
:::

## The three stages of coalescence

When a water droplet falls into a pool of water, it does not instantly merge or "dissolve". Because liquid water is composed of the same chemical species, this is not chemical solute dissolution, but **hydrodynamic coalescence**.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Falling Droplet
    participant F as Nanoscale Air Cushion
    participant P as Bulk Liquid Pool
    
    D->>F: 1. Impact and deformation (Hovering stage)
    F-->>D: Squeezes air out via lubrication flow
    Note over D,P: 2. Film thins below 10-50 nm (van der Waals collapse)
    D->>P: 3. Film ruptures and a capillary bridge nucleates
    P->>D: 4. Capillary recoil drives upward capillary waves
    D->>P: 5. Partial pinch-off: Daughter droplet ejected (Cascade)
```

### Lubrication-limited air drainage

As the droplet approaches the free liquid surface, it traps a microscopic layer of air. The droplet cannot touch the pool until this gas cushion is drained laterally.

The drainage velocity $u(r)$ of the gas layer of thickness $h(t)$ is governed by the Reynolds lubrication equation:

$$\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{12 \mu_{\text{air}}} \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r h^3 \frac{\partial P}{\partial r} \right)$$

where $\mu_{\text{air}}$ is dynamic air viscosity ($1.81 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa s}$). This lubrication resistance allows millimeter-sized droplets to bounce or skim across the surface for tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

### Capillary bridge formation

When drainage thins the air layer below roughly $10\text{ to }50\text{ nm}$, long-range attractive van der Waals forces destabilize the interface. The film ruptures at a single point, creating a microscopic liquid neck (the **capillary bridge**).

The bridge has an extremely sharp negative radius of curvature ($r_{\text{neck}}$), generating an intense localized capillary suction pressure:

$$\Delta P_{\text{bridge}} \sim -\frac{\gamma}{r_{\text{neck}}}$$

This suction accelerates fluid across the neck at velocities exceeding $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, rapidly widening the bridge according to the hydrodynamic scaling law:

$$r_{\text{neck}}(t) \propto \left( \frac{\gamma R_0}{\rho} \right)^{1/4} t^{1/2}$$

The bridge radius $r_{\text{neck}}$ (magenta) carries extreme curvature, so the Laplace pressure driving it open is initially enormous — the neck widens in an inertially limited regime rather than a viscous one, and the interface reorganises far faster than the drop as a whole can respond.</figcaption>
```{=html}
</figure>
```


### The partial coalescence cascade

As fluid drains into the bulk, capillary waves propagate upward along the droplet surface. 

```{=html}
<figure markdown="span">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 216" style="width:100%;max-width:760px;height:auto;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif;" role="img" aria-label="Four stages of partial coalescence: bridge formation, capillary waves converging, neck pinch-off, and a daughter droplet.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="wdL" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="7" refX="8" refY="3.5" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0, 9 3.5, 0 7" fill="var(--ink-rust)"/></marker>
    <marker id="wdN" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="6" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><polygon points="0 0, 7 3, 0 6" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)"/></marker>
  </defs>

    <text x="402" y="40" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color)" font-size="14" font-weight="600">c  Neck pinches off</text>
  <text x="402" y="196" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12">vertical column severs</text>
  <path d="M 388 96 C 388 70, 416 70, 416 96 C 416 112, 408 116, 406 122 L 398 122 C 396 116, 388 112, 388 96 Z" fill="var(--ink-indigo)" fill-opacity="0.16" stroke="var(--md-default-fg-color)" stroke-width="2.2"/>
  <path d="M 396 126 q 6 8 12 0" fill="none" stroke="var(--ink-rust)" stroke-width="2.4"/>
  <line x1="402" y1="146" x2="402" y2="132" stroke="var(--ink-rust)" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#wdL)"/>
    <text x="602" y="40" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color)" font-size="14" font-weight="600">d  Daughter drop</text>
  <text x="602" y="196" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--md-default-fg-color--light)" font-size="12">a smaller drop rebounds; the cascade repeats</text>
  <circle cx="602" cy="92" r="17" fill="var(--ink-indigo)" fill-opacity="0.16" stroke="var(--md-default-fg-color)" stroke-width="2.2"/>
  <path d="M 578 150 q 24 -12 48 0" fill="none" stroke="var(--md-default-fg-color)" stroke-width="2" opacity="0.55"/>
</svg>
<figcaption><strong>Figure 3 | Coalescence is often partial: the drop leaves a smaller copy of itself behind.</strong> <strong>a</strong>, The bridge opens. <strong>b</strong>, Capillary waves generated at the neck race up the drop surface and converge at its apex (magenta). <strong>c</strong>, Their convergence pulls the drop into a vertical column whose neck pinches off before the volume has finished draining. <strong>d</strong>, What separates is a daughter droplet roughly half the parent diameter, which can repeat the whole sequence — a self-similar cascade that continues until viscosity finally dominates and merging completes.</figcaption>
</figure>
```


1. The converging capillary waves meet at the top apex of the droplet.
2. The downward drainage momentum competes with the horizontal capillary pinch-off.
3. If the **Ohnesorge number** ($Oh = \mu / \sqrt{\rho \gamma R_0}$) is below a critical threshold ($Oh \lesssim 0.026$), inertia dominates viscous dissipation. The bottom of the droplet drains into the pool, but the top portion pinches off, ejecting a **daughter droplet** with roughly $50\%$ of the parent droplet's diameter.
4. This daughter droplet falls back onto the surface, traps a new air film, and repeats the cycle. Under clean conditions, a single water droplet can undergo **4 to 6 successive cascade steps** before viscous damping halts the cascade and complete absorption into a submerged vortex ring occurs.

## Dimensionless numbers

| Dimensionless Group | Formula | Physical Interpretation | Regime Transition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Weber Number ($We$)** | $\frac{\rho_a v^2 d}{\gamma}$ | Inertial drag force vs Surface tension force | $We > 12 \implies$ Droplet bag breakup |
| **Bond / Eötvös Number ($Bo$)** | $\frac{\Delta \rho g d^2}{\gamma}$ | Gravitational body force vs Surface tension force | $Bo \ll 1 \implies$ Spherical geometry dominates |
| **Ohnesorge Number ($Oh$)** | $\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\rho \gamma d}}$ | Viscous dissipation vs Capillary-inertial forces | $Oh < 0.026 \implies$ Partial coalescence cascade occurs |
| **Capillary Number ($Ca$)** | $\frac{\mu v}{\gamma}$ | Viscous shear stress vs Interfacial tension | $Ca \gg 1 \implies$ Viscous elongation and breakup |

## Key takeaways

- A drop meeting a pool first meets a film of air; the Reynolds lubrication equation makes drainage slow as $h^3$, so millimetre drops hover or bounce for tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
- Below $10$ to $50\text{ nm}$ van der Waals forces rupture the film and a capillary bridge nucleates; its extreme curvature drives the neck open at over $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, with $r_{\text{neck}} \propto t^{1/2}$.
- Capillary waves converging at the drop apex can pinch off a daughter drop about half the parent diameter if $Oh \lesssim 0.026$; the cascade repeats four to six times before viscosity ends it.
- The Weber, Bond, Ohnesorge and capillary numbers each compare surface tension against one competing stress, and each has a threshold that marks a change of regime.
